newsitem.title: USA: Albright aims for active U.S. diplomacy.
newsitem.headline: Albright aims for active U.S. diplomacy.

text.p: Secretary of State-designate Madeleine Albright promised at her Senate confirmation hearing on Wednesday to create a strong, active diplomacy and work to make the United States a "dynamic hub of the global economy."

Albright, President Bill Clinton's nominee to be the first woman secretary of state, said Washington would do more to reduce tensions in Cyprus, India-Pakistan and Nagorno-Karabakh and maintain its central role in Middle East peace efforts and its involvement in Northern Ireland peace moves.

In testimony to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, she also said she "would not hestitate to address frankly" human rights abuses, including those in China, although America's focus would be "Chinese integration, not isolation."

She promised an early trip to Asia -- citing Japan and South Korea as two stops -- and said developing strong bilateral ties with China was a priority. But officials said her first overseas travel would be to Europe in February.
She also stressed the importance of proceeding with NATO expansion and building close ties with Russia and Ukraine.

Albright, who fled to the United States from her native Czechoslovakia after the Second World War, was introduced to the panel by outgoing Secretary of State Warren Christopher, who called her a "magnificent choice" as his successor.
The hearing was a love feast. Senators welcomed her warmly and few pressed hard on policy issues.

Sen. Jesse Helms, Republican chairman, said the panel would meet on Jan. 20, the day Clinton is inaugurated -- or maybe earlier if possible -- and approve her appointment. The full Senate would then confirm her on Jan. 21, another senator said.

Albright, Washington's outgoing U.N. ambassador, made an emphatic pitch to Congress, which forced big foreign affairs spending cuts in recent years, to restore funding, saying the United States needs first-class diplomacy. "Force alone can be a blunt instrument and there are many problems it cannot solve," she said.

"We must be the authors of the history of our age," Albright told the committee, adding: "Our leadership must be sustained if our interests are to be protected around the world ... We cannot have that on the cheap. We must invest the resources needed to maintain American leadership."

She said the United States is "the world's richest, strongest, most respected nation (yet) provides a smaller percentage of our wealth to support democracy and growth in the developing world than any other industrialised nation."

She said she had "an open mind" on merging the Agency for International Development and two other independent agencies into the State Department -- a restructuring many say must happen if Congress is to increase foreign affairs spending.

But while stressing U.S. leadership must be sustained to protect U.S. global interests, she also said, "We do not have unlimited resources, nor do we have unlimited responsibilities ... We have to weigh our commitments carefully."

She would never advise deploying U.S. troops overseas "where other means are available, where there is not support from Congress and the American people ... and where there is not the likihood or reality of winning," she said.
Albright vowed to promote a fair world trading system and make the United States a "dynamic hub of the global economy."

The administration would place "high priority" on Chile's early addition to the North American Free Trade Agreement on "equitable terms" and on the extension to Central America and the Caribbean of "arrangements equivalent to NAFTA," she said.
Another priority was quick Senate approval of the long-delayed chemical weapons convention, she said.

Albright said Washington would increase efforts to resolve tensions in Cyprus, divided between Greeks and Turks since 1974. On India and Pakistan, which have nuclear programmes, she said, "We will again consider the prospects for reducing the tensions."

She said Washington was prepared to play "a more visible role" to settle the disputed enclave of Nagorno-Karabakh, and suggested Congress could boost U.S. influence by lifting limits on nonmilitary assistance to Azerbaijan, while maintaining aid for Armenia.
She backed the long-delayed Hebron deal under negotiation by Israel and the Palestinians saying it would "serve as a catalyst, strengthening the supporters of peace."
The proceedings were interrupted when several protestors shouted out concerns about the effect on Iraqi children of U.S.-led international sanctions. They were quickly escorted from the hearing room.
